summary.text: 文 is described in early forms as a human-shaped graph bearing marks on the chest. The marks’ referent and the graph’s earliest meaning remain disputed.

formation.text: The graph is analyzed as a pictograph of a whole standing human figure, not as a compound of separate modern-looking parts. The chest marks have been read as tattooing or other marking; a competing proposal interprets 文 as “great” in some early contexts. The original referent is unresolved.

history.text: 文 is reported in Late Shang oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions. Accounts of later bronze forms describe chest marks reduced to dots or short strokes, and sometimes absent. Forms are also indexed in Chu manuscripts and small-seal script; these categories do not establish a direct sequence between every surviving form.

The Han-dynasty Shuowen account explains 文 through crossed markings or interwoven pattern. This is an interpretation of the seal form, not independent evidence for what the earlier chest marks represented.

uncertainties.text: The chest marks have been interpreted as tattooing, other body marking, or garment-related marks. Another proposal reads 文 as corresponding to 大 and meaning “great” in some Shang contexts. These accounts remain disputed.
The exact first inscriptional instance and its date are unresolved. The evidence does not establish a dated progression from early marking or “great” to pattern, writing, literature, and culture.
The proposed relationship to 紋 and proposed derivation from 煤 are not substantiated by the evidence provided.

senses.gloss: use in names and as an honorific modifier
senses.period: Late Shang; exact first instance unresolved
senses.text: The earliest uses reported here occur in personal and place names, especially as an honorific modifier in royal names. This use does not establish the graph’s original meaning; “great” is one proposed interpretation.

senses.gloss: honorific use in royal posthumous names and for ancestors
senses.text: 文 is reported in royal posthumous names and ancestor honorifics in Western Zhou bronze inscriptions.
Writing, literature, and culture are documented meanings of 文. The evidence does not date their emergence or establish a progression among them.
The Shuowen account interprets 文 through crossed markings or interwoven pattern. It describes the seal form, rather than proving the referent of the Shang graph.

limitations.text: The reported early honorific use and the current meanings do not establish a semantic link. No dated chain connects the proposed chest marking or “great” interpretation to pattern, writing, literature, and culture.

overview.text: 文 is a whole human-shaped graph, described in early forms with marks on the chest. Their meaning and the graph’s earliest sense remain disputed.
